sound.text: Ear Candi came out in June 2020, weeks after George Floyd was killed, and its cover comes from the protests that followed. SyWavy had a lot on his mind that summer. The sound picked up where Keys' left off: Keys' was built on a single sample, so Jett2Fly kept building beats from samples and loops. They made far more songs that year than they ever released, and these five are the ones they kept.

notes.title: I've Got the Joy
notes.body: The Sunday school song I've Got the Joy, Joy, Joy, Joy (Down in My Heart). The song's title, the joy piled on joy and the gospel sample all point back to it, with his soul in place of the heart.

ref.name: I've Got the Joy (Sunday school song)

notes.body: He recorded this on an iPhone 8 he was using as a burner, a cheap spare phone.
CR is short for copyright, as in owning the rights to his music. There was no graduation, but he might get his songs copyrighted, and he's willing to wait for it.

notes.title: Kids' Choice Awards
notes.body: Nickelodeon's yearly awards show, where kids vote for the winners. The kid and choice together make its name, and Timmy Turner, from another Nickelodeon show, turns up later in the song.

notes.title: Future
notes.body: The Atlanta rapper hides in the line: seeing the future is also seeing Future.

notes.title: J. Cole
notes.body: Fayetteville, North Carolina, J. Cole's hometown, goes by the Ville, and Forbidden Fruit is a song from his 2013 album Born Sinner. The trip and the fruit both come from him.

notes.title: Gravity Falls
notes.body: The Disney cartoon about twins Dipper and Mabel Pines spending a summer in a strange Oregon town. Leaving becomes a pun on Dipper's name, which makes Mabel his sister.
The opener lays out where he stands: he answers to himself, no genre fits him, and a choir sample sits under everything. Everyone else is reaching for something that comes naturally to him.
The title comes into focus here: joy, and gratitude that he never quit making music. He even makes room for the people who will hate on him, and admits he'd feel the same way in their place.

notes.title: Triller
notes.body: The short video app that courted musicians in 2020 as a TikTok rival. A snippet posted there doubles as calling the song a thriller.

notes.title: Bryson Tiller
notes.body: The Louisville R&B singer whose 2015 debut, Trapsoul, made his name. He folds that album and one of its biggest singles into back-to-back lines.

notes.title: Five Pillars of Islam
notes.body: The five core practices of Islam: the declaration of faith, daily prayer, charity, fasting during Ramadan, and the pilgrimage to Mecca.

notes.title: Flashing Lights
notes.body: Kanye West's 2007 single from his album Graduation. The next line turns that album's title into a joke about his own schooling.

notes.title: Boy Meets World
notes.body: The 90s sitcom where Cory Matthews and Topanga Lawrence grow from classmates into a married couple. He casts himself as Cory, with a Topanga of his own.

notes.title: Timmy Turner
notes.body: The kid from Nickelodeon's The Fairly OddParents, known for his big pink cap. His own hat would never sit like that.
He comes back to the sample, a gospel record, and makes clear the joy runs deep. There was no blueprint to copy either: he built the song out of his own life.

notes.title: Good Morning
notes.body: The opening track on Kanye West's Graduation, the album he joked about earlier in the song. Coming first is what this song and that one have in common.
Smeez is slang for fake or messy people, and he keeps his distance from them.

notes.title: Sour Patch Kids
notes.body: Patch and sour make Sour Patch Kids, the candy, on an EP called Ear Candi.

notes.title: The Weeknd
notes.body: The Toronto singer's fourth album came out in March 2020, three months before this EP, and its title runs through the hook. The song's own title spells weekend his way.
He turns on someone who acts like family but isn't, and the way they've treated him feels strange to him. The pun between family and familiar carries the verse.

notes.title: What a Time to Be Alive
notes.body: Drake and Future's 2015 joint mixtape. Live From the Gutter is one of its songs, so the line names the tape and a track off it.

ref.name: What a Time to Be Alive

notes.title: Tory Burch
notes.body: The American fashion label known for flats and sandals with a double T logo. Her pair is a yellow shade.

notes.title: Sneaky link
notes.body: Slang for someone you hook up with in secret. The phrase spread across social media in 2020, the year this came out.
In the middle of the party talk, he asks what she cares about beyond the party and she comes up empty. That one exchange turns a weekend song into a picture of someone he can't reach.

notes.title: Heartless
notes.body: One of the first singles from The Weeknd's After Hours, the album the hook keeps naming. He flips its title around and calls himself the opposite.
The line plays miss two ways: never missing a shot, and missing a person. He's good at the first and stuck on the second.

notes.title: Dennis the Menace
notes.body: Hank Ketcham's comic strip kid who leaves trouble everywhere he goes. She's no more blameless than Dennis.
Time stands still, every argument goes nowhere, and what's left of the relationship sits in old texts. Phones as the place where love fades out becomes a thread through his music.
This early on, he's already the one behind the camera for his own visuals. Directing has stayed part of what he does, alongside the music he makes with Jett2Fly.

notes.title: 30 for 30
notes.body: ESPN's sports documentary series, running since 2009. He's just watched one.

notes.title: Julius Erving
notes.body: Dr. J, the Hall of Fame forward who starred for the New York Nets and the Philadelphia 76ers, as famous for his afro as his dunks. His own hair earns the comparison.

notes.title: Speckles
notes.body: The star-nosed mole from Disney's 2009 movie G-Force, the team's computer expert, voiced by Nicolas Cage. Moles live underground, so coming up from the underground makes him like Speckles.

notes.title: Aston Martin
notes.body: The British luxury car maker. He stretches its name across two lines, sound by sound.
He's moving fast here, with new music and beats that hit hard. He also nods to Keys', his single from that March, now finished and locked away.

notes.title: World's smallest violin
notes.body: The joke of rubbing two fingers together to play a tiny violin for someone's sob story. He plays one for a sad story, which means he isn't moved.

notes.title: Jawn
notes.body: Philadelphia slang that can stand in for almost any noun. Here it means people he used to know.
People ask where the beats come from, and he shuts down the idea that they're free beats off YouTube. They're Jett2Fly's, which is why the next line calls the two of them a buddy movie.

notes.title: Rush Hour
notes.body: The 1998 action comedy that paired Jackie Chan and Chris Tucker as mismatched partners. That's his working relationship with Jett2Fly: two different styles that click.

notes.title: Austin Powers
notes.body: Mike Myers' spy parody series, soaked in loud 1960s colors and patterns. Groovy is the hero's favorite word, and it's the one he picks for what he's wearing.

notes.title: The Matrix
notes.body: The 1999 sci-fi film, famous for Neo bending backward to dodge bullets in a long black coat. He strikes the same pose in photos.

notes.title: Miami Hurricanes
notes.body: The University of Miami's teams, named for the storms that hit South Florida, and the line means both. The weather keeps going on the next line, with everything coming down like rain.

notes.title: OVO
notes.body: October's Very Own, Drake's label and clothing line, known for its owl logo.

notes.title: Virgil Abloh
notes.body: The designer who founded Off-White and later led menswear at Louis Vuitton. He died in 2021. The blazer is a sneaker, the Nike Blazer Mid that Abloh redesigned for The Ten, his 2017 collection with Nike, and Jett2Fly owns a pair. So the line works two ways: Abloh made the shoe, and SyWavy's producer is wearing Abloh.

notes.title: Jack Sparrow
notes.body: Johnny Depp's pirate captain in the Pirates of the Caribbean films. His first name doubles as getting robbed.

notes.title: Tupac Shakur
notes.body: 2Pac's 1998 single Changes, built over Bruce Hornsby's The Way It Is, opens with nearly the same complaint. Here it's pointed at a woman who keeps going back to the wrong guys.

notes.title: Tory Lanez
notes.body: The Toronto singer and rapper. His name splits across the line to tell someone they're out of place.

notes.title: Smino
notes.body: The St. Louis artist known for flows that speed up and slow down mid-verse. Switching the tempo is the move he's borrowing.

notes.title: Kinko's
notes.body: The copy shop chain, now FedEx Office. Even a copy shop couldn't make another one of him.
He plays heartbreak cool: a shrug, a love he can't shake, a breakup he admits anyone can see on him. The shrug comes back at the end of the song, aimed at everyone.
Here the hook points at someone else's music: he listens to their latest and finds the same old thing. His own newest work is a different story, and she can't stop looking.

notes.title: Living Single
notes.body: The 90s Fox sitcom about friends in a Brooklyn brownstone. Synclaire's sweetheart was the building's handyman Overton, so the line packs both of them and the show's title into a few words.

notes.title: Moncler
notes.body: The luxury label from the French Alps, best known for its down puffer jackets. He's freezing without one.
